summary: Proposes a standard syntax for Network Standard Data Pathnames: a uniform way to say where a collection of bits lives on the network. It was replaced by RFC 645.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 615 proposes a common way to write a data pathname for locations on the ARPA Network. The format uses named fields so users and programs do not need to remember every site's local pathname style.

questions: what is a network standard data pathname
what fields are in the nsdp format
subtitle: A proposed syntax for naming data locations across the ARPA Network.

tldr.problem: Users and programs working across network sites faced different local pathname conventions and needed a shared syntax for referring to data locations.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal defines percent-prefixed pathnames with keyed fields for network, host, peripheral, directory, file, type, and site-specific parameters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 615 is a proposed pathname syntax and was obsoleted by RFC 645.

today: RFC 615 is a proposed Network Standard Data Pathname syntax and was obsoleted by RFC 645.

sections.title: A Network Standard Data Pathname
sections.content:
The memo proposes a Network Standard Data Pathname (NSDP): a standardized way to refer to a location for a collection of bits somewhere on the Network. It is intended for users who work at several sites, programs that access data at multiple sites, and documentation.

The RFC proposes a pathname syntax only. It says the format allows fields for the network, host, peripheral device, directory, file, type, and site-specific information.
sections.plainLanguage: Different sites used different ways to name files. This proposal gives users and programs a shared format for describing a data location.

sections.title: Fields and Delimiters
sections.content:
An NSDP starts with a percent sign and contains fields. Each field has a key, a left delimiter, a name, and a right delimiter. The keys can be full words or single-character forms: NETWORK/N, HOST/H, PERIPHERAL/P, DIRECTORY/D, FILE/F, TYPE/T, and SITEPARM/S.

Fields are order-dependent and may repeat where the destination site allows it. Delimiters mark the start and end of each name; matching brackets should be used when the left delimiter is an opening bracket.
sections.plainLanguage: Each field says what its following name means, such as the host, directory, or file. The fields have an order, and the delimiters show where each name begins and ends.

sections.title: Field Meanings and Defaults
sections.content:
The Network field currently defines only ARPA. A Host can be named by its official name, nickname, or number. Peripheral identifies a device; Directory identifies a directory; File gives the basic file or data-set name; Type is an optional filename modifier; and Siteparm carries parameters defined by the destination site.

The memo offers context-dependent defaults as guidelines: Network defaults to ARPA, Host to the host interpreting the pathname, Peripheral to ONLINE, Directory to the user's current working directory, and Filename, Type, and Siteparm have no default. The RFC notes that the syntax does not address data smaller than a file.
sections.plainLanguage: The fields identify the network, host, storage device, directory, and file. Some fields have suggested defaults, and each site decides which combinations it accepts.
